Toady

TOH-dee · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Toady is a person who flatters and behaves in a groveling way toward someone powerful, hoping for favor.

Historians describe the minister as a toady who never once contradicted the emperor.

Worked Example

Everyone in the office rolled their eyes at the new toady who agreed with every word the manager said.

Agreeing with every single word the manager says is exactly toady behavior.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

yes-man: a person who always agrees to please someone in authority

bootlicker: an excessively groveling flatterer

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

critic: a person who openly judges or disagrees

Where it sits · how groveling the flattery becomes — fan → toady → sycophant

fan vs. toady: A fan admires someone sincerely from a distance; a toady flatters directly and specifically to gain personal advantage.

sycophant vs. toady: Sycophant (taught in this same unit) is the more classical, formal term for the same flattering behavior; toady is the more casual, everyday word for the same kind of person.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Toady is shortened from 'toad-eater,' the old name for a traveling quack doctor's assistant, who would pretend to eat a toad (believed poisonous) so the quack doctor could dramatically 'cure' him in front of a crowd.

Use the root in a new word: toad-eater

Use the root in a new word: toad-eater: The full original phrase, toad-eater, survived into the 1800s before shortening to today's toady -- one of the more surprising word histories in this entire course.

Word Building

Toady is a somewhat contemptuous, informal noun for a specific person who behaves in a groveling way toward one powerful figure, distinct from Sycophant (taught in this same unit), the more classical term for the same flattering role.
